notes_title: Chat assistants write fluent text, and some of it is false. Today you'll see what a language model does, why it can invent a confident answer, and how to fix that by finding the right passage first. We'll build the search ourselves, in plain Python, over the eight Lakeside Mart policy documents, and then test it with a sheet of twelve questions. Everything runs free in your own notebook.
notes_outcomes: You'll explain tokens, context and next word prediction in plain words, build retrieval over a handful of documents so that a question finds the right passage, and test the answers against a checked list, recording every failure. The test sheet sits in the middle of the two hours, and the lab is built around it. The small model that writes the final answer comes last, and it is optional.
notes_words: Seven words today, and they cover how a model writes and how we check it. A token is a piece of text a model reads, like one cell of a long row. A prompt is the instruction you type. The context is everything the model can see when it answers, a bit like the range a formula reads. A hallucination is a confident answer with no fact behind it. Retrieval is finding the right passage first, much like a lookup. A passage is one short piece of a document. A use log records what an assistant gave you and how you checked it.

slides.title: Warm-up from Session 21

questions.q: Why does a computer need our text turned into numbers before it can compare two messages?
questions.a: It only works with numbers. Counts of words or an embedding give each message a position it can measure.

questions.q: You searched for a long queue at the till and found messages with different words. How?
questions.a: Embeddings put messages with a similar meaning close together, so the search follows meaning and not exact words.

slides.notes:
Last session we turned text into numbers. Two questions on that before we move on.

First. Why does a computer need our text turned into numbers before it can compare two messages? Take your time.

It only works with numbers. So we gave each message a set of numbers, either counts of words or an embedding, and then the computer could measure how close two messages are.

Second. You searched for a long queue at the till and found messages that used different words. How did that work? Have a think.

Embeddings put messages with a similar meaning close together. The search follows meaning and ignores the exact words. Today we use that same idea to build something people use every day, a tool that answers questions from your own documents.

slides.title: A language model predicts the next token
slides.lead: Everything a language model writes comes from one repeated guess. What piece of text most likely comes next?

points.t: A word or a piece of a word. Each one has a number.
The model scores every possible next token and picks one.
It learned these scores by reading a very large amount of text.

slides.alt: A sentence split into word and word-piece boxes, each with an identification number underneath.
slides.notes:
Let's start with what a language model does. It predicts the next token.

A token is a word, or a piece of a word. Look at the picture. The word provider is cut into two pieces, pro and vider. Each piece has a number underneath. The numbers in this picture are made up to show the idea. A real model has its own list.

Given the tokens so far, the model gives a score to every token it knows, and then picks one. It learned those scores by reading a huge amount of text.

That's all it does. It has no spreadsheet of facts inside and no list of Lakeside Mart rules. It has learned what text tends to follow what text.

slides.title: One answer is built one token at a time

steps.t: It scores every possible next token.
That token joins the text so far.
It goes round again until it stops.

slides.caption: An answer of forty tokens means forty trips round this loop.
slides.notes:
Here's the loop that produces every answer you've ever seen from a chat assistant.

First the model reads your prompt. A prompt is the text you give it.

Second, it scores every token it knows as a possible next piece.

Third, it picks one. Usually a likely one, and sometimes a surprising one, which is why the same question can get two different answers.

Fourth, the chosen token is added to the text so far.

Fifth, it goes round again, now with one more token to read. It keeps going until it produces a token that means stop.

So a long answer is just a lot of small guesses in a row. Each guess is made by looking at everything written so far.

slides.title: The same model with a vague prompt and a clear prompt

points: The model fills the gaps itself
You are a till assistant. Using the text below, say how many days a customer has to return an item.
The text below is the context

slides.verdict: A prompt is an instruction. Everything the model can see when it answers is the context.
slides.notes:
Same model, two prompts. A prompt is the instruction you give it, in plain words.

On the left, a vague one. Tell me about returns. The model has to guess who's asking, what they want and where the facts come from, and it fills every gap itself.

On the right, a clear one. It gives the model a role, a task, and a limit. It says use the text below. That text is part of what the model can see.

Everything the model can see when it answers is called the context. Your prompt, the text you paste in, and the answer so far, all sit inside it. The model can only use what's inside the context, plus whatever it learned in training. That second part is where the trouble starts.

slides.title: Models invent because they predict likely text
slides.lead: When a model has no fact in its context, it still writes something. That something is called a hallucination.

points.t: The answer reads well and sounds sure.
Nothing inside the model looks the fact up.
A likely number or date gets written even if it is wrong.

slides.notes:
The trouble starts here. A language model writes the most likely text. It doesn't look anything up.

So suppose you ask it how long loyalty points last at Lakeside Mart. It has never seen our policy, because the policy is ours. It still has to produce a next token, and then another. So it writes a likely answer, such as a number of months that points often last in other shops.

The answer reads well. It sounds sure. And it can be wrong. When a model writes a confident answer that isn't backed by any fact in front of it, we call it a hallucination.

In spreadsheet terms, it's a formula that returns a clean looking number with no data behind it. The cure is to put the fact in the context before the model answers.

slides.title: A confident answer with no source
slides.looks: You ask a model how long Lakeside Mart loyalty points last. It answers in one smooth sentence with a specific number of months. Nothing warns you.
slides.why: Our policy was never in its context, so the number is a likely guess. A smooth sentence says nothing about whether it is true.
slides.fix: Make the model answer from your document, show the passage it used, and check the answer against that passage.
slides.notes:
This trap runs with no error at all.

You ask for the loyalty points rule. You get a neat sentence with a specific number of months in it. It looks like the work of someone who knows.

The model never saw our policy. The number is a likely guess dressed as a fact. How would you spot that, if you didn't already know the answer? Sit with it for a second.

You wouldn't, from the answer alone. The sentence is equally smooth when it's right and when it's wrong.

So the fix has three parts. Make the model answer from your own document. Show the passage it used beside the answer. And check the answer against that passage. The real policy says points expire after twelve months, and we'll find that line in code in a few minutes.

slides.title: Retrieval first, then the model answers
look: The question goes in first and is turned into numbers.
Your documents are searched for the closest passages.
The model answers from those passages and shows its source.
slides.caption: Retrieval means finding the right passage before anyone answers.
slides.alt: Pipeline: a question becomes a vector, the closest document passages are found, and a language model answers using only those passages.
slides.notes:
This is the pattern for the rest of the session. Retrieval before answering. Retrieval means finding the right passage first. A passage is a short piece of a document, here a sentence or two.

The question comes in and is turned into something we can compare. In Session 21 that was an embedding. Today we start with something simpler.

Then we search our own documents for the passages closest to the question. Those are the ones the question is most likely about.

Last, the model answers from those passages, and we show the source beside the answer. The person reading can check it in ten seconds.

In the Excel world this is a lookup first, and a sentence written around the result second. The lookup is the part we can test.

slides.title: Split eight policies into passages
slides.code:
import os, re
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

passages = []
for name in sorted(os.listdir('policies')):
    text = ' '.join(open('policies/' + name).read().split())
    for s in re.split(r'(?<=\.)\s+(?=[A-Z])', text):
        passages.append((name, s))
print(len(passages), 'passages')
print(passages[28])
says: Read each policy file and tidy the spaces.
Cut each file after a full stop. Each piece is a passage.
Keep the file name with every passage, so we can cite the source.
slides.notes:
Let's build retrieval with nothing but Python and NumPy. First, our documents. Lakeside Mart has eight policy files in a folder called policies. Returns, loyalty, mobile money, delivery, food safety, data privacy, opening hours and supplier quality.

We read each file and tidy the spacing.

Then we cut each file into sentences. Every file is a single block of text, so a sentence is the natural size for a passage. The cut happens after a full stop that's followed by a capital letter.

We keep the file name beside every passage. That's our source. When the program answers, it can say where the answer came from.

The result is fifty nine passages. The one we printed is a short one from the loyalty policy. Points expire after twelve months.

slides.title: Score by shared words and return the best passage
slides.code:
FILLER = set('the a an of to in is are do does how what '
  'can my for on at and or it be by with if we you from '
  'when which will i'.split())
def words(text):
    w = re.findall('[a-z0-9]+', text.lower())
    return {x for x in w if x not in FILLER}
def retrieve(question):
    q = words(question)
    sc = [len(q & words(p)) for n, p in passages]
    i = int(np.argmax(sc))
    return passages[i], sc[i]
best, score = retrieve('How long do points last?')
print(best[0], score)
print(best[1][:34])

Data is kept for 3 years after the
says: Throw away filler words such as the and of, and keep the rest.
A passage scores one point for each word it shares with the question.
argmax picks the passage with the top score.
slides.notes:
The first search is the simplest method I know. Count the words the question shares with each passage, and return the passage with the most.

First we make a short list of filler words, such as the, of and how. They appear everywhere and tell us nothing, so we throw them away.

Then each passage gets one point for every remaining word it shares with the question. NumPy's argmax gives us the position of the highest score.

We ask our question. How long do points last?

The answer comes from the data privacy policy. Data is kept for three years after the last purchase. It scored one point, for the word last. The method found a passage that shares a word with the question, and that passage answers a different question.

Nothing crashed. It just retrieved the wrong thing. That's why we test.

slides.title: Tune the search: same meaning, rare words count more
slides.output:
loyalty_programme.txt Points expire after 12 months.
weighted score: 0.7
says: Treat last and expire as the same word, and cut a trailing s.
A word found in few passages is worth more than a word found in many.
Same question. Now the loyalty passage wins.
slides.notes:
So we tune the method, with two small changes.

First, a tiny list of words that mean the same. Last and expire. Customers say last, the policy says expire. We also cut a trailing s, so points and point match.

Second, rare words count for more. A word that appears in only one or two passages tells us a lot. A word that appears in twenty tells us little. So each shared word scores one divided by the number of passages that contain it. You may remember that idea from Session 21.

Now the same question gives the right sentence. Points expire after twelve months. The score is about zero point seven.

We looked at a failure, worked out why it failed, and changed the method. The questions stayed as they were. That is the fair way to tune.

slides.caption: Twelve questions in all. The simple method picks the right policy 11 times and finds the answer 10 times. The tuned method gets 12 of 12.
slides.notes:
The test sheet is a table. Each row has a question, the policy that should answer it, and the exact words of the correct answer, copied from the policy file. Then we add what our program returned, whether the answer was found, and a failures column that says what went wrong.

Here are four of the twelve rows. The first two are failures. The points question went to the wrong policy. The data question found the right policy and the wrong sentence. The third and fourth passed.

Across all twelve, the simple method picks the right policy eleven times and finds the answer itself ten times. The tuned method gets all twelve.

The failures column tells you what to fix next.

Be fair with yourself though. We tuned on these twelve, so a fresh set of questions may do worse. Keep a few questions hidden for that reason.

slides.title: Search by meaning with sentence-transformers
slides.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
vectors = model.encode([p for n, p in passages], normalize_embeddings=True)

def retrieve3(question):
    qv = model.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    scores = vectors @ qv
    i = int(scores.argmax())
    return passages[i], round(float(scores[i]), 2)

retrieve3('How long do points last?')
says: Load the small model from Session 21. It runs inside Colab.
Encode every passage once, then compare by a dot product.
slides.notes:
This version searches by meaning, with the model from Session 21. You'll run it in Colab, and the numbers will be your own.

We load the small sentence model, the same one as last session. It downloads once, about ninety megabytes, and then runs inside your notebook. No key, no account, nothing sent anywhere.

We turn every passage into a vector once, which is the list of numbers we called an embedding last session. For a question, we turn it into a vector too, and compare it with all of them using a dot product. Because the vectors are scaled to the same length, the biggest dot product means the closest meaning.

This method doesn't need a list of words that mean the same. A question with the word last should land near a passage with the word expire. Test it on your twelve questions and see.

slides.title: Let a small model write the answer
slides.code:
from transformers import pipeline
generate = pipeline('text-generation',
    model='Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct')
RULE = 'Answer only from the passage. Else say so.'
def answer(question):
    (name, passage), s = retrieve2(question)
    text = f'Passage: {passage}\nQuestion: {question}'
    msgs = [{'role': 'system', 'content': RULE},
            {'role': 'user', 'content': text}]
    out = generate(msgs, max_new_tokens=60,
                   do_sample=False)
    return out[0]['generated_text'][-1]['content']
print(answer('How long do points last?'))
says: Load a small open model that runs on the Colab processor.
Give it the passage and a rule: answer only from the passage.
Print the reply. Check it against the passage yourself.
slides.notes:
The last step is the model. Again you'll run this in Colab. It's optional. The session works with retrieval alone.

We load a small open model. This one is about half a billion parameters, small enough to run on the free Colab processor, slowly. It downloads once into your notebook.

The function finds the best passage with our own search, then sends the model two messages. The first sets a rule. Answer only from the passage, and say so if the answer isn't there. The second holds the passage and the question.

We turn off random choice, so the same question gives the same answer each time.

The reply could still be wrong or oddly worded. A small model is weaker than the large ones you read about. So you test it the same way, with your twelve questions, and you record every failure.

A word about where all this runs.

The small model is downloaded into your Colab notebook and runs there. We don't call a hosted service. There's no key to paste in and no account to pay for. Nothing you type is sent to a company that sells model access.

Every model comes with a card that states its licence. Before class I read the card for the model we use and confirm that we're allowed to use it this way. Do the same any time you pick a model. The licence says what you may do with it, and some models forbid commercial use.

And it's optional. If your notebook is slow or the download fails, you still have retrieval and the test sheet, and that's where most of the skill is.

rows: Said a column name had a typo
A split on every full stop

slides.caption: Keep a use log. A free assistant is optional, and you stay responsible for every line.
slides.notes:
You may use a free chat assistant to help with code. It's optional, and I'd like you to use it in three steps. Use, check and record.

Use it. Ask it to explain an error, or draft a function.

Check it. Run the code. Test it on a case where you already know the answer. Never paste in code you haven't read. An assistant can write code that runs and gives the wrong result, exactly like the wrong passage we saw earlier.

Record it. Keep a small table. What you asked, what it gave, how you checked, and whether you kept it.

Look at the example rows. In the third one the suggestion failed the check, and the log says so. That record is useful to you next month, and useful to anyone who reviews your work.

slides.title: Do not paste customer data into tools you do not control
slides.lead: Our policy and the Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019 both ask for care with personal data.

points.t: If you do not control where the text goes, do not paste customer data.
Share counts and customer numbers, never names or phone numbers.
Practise on fictional data, as we do in this course.

slides.notes:
One rule matters more than any other today. Don't paste customer data into any tool you don't control.

That means a free chat assistant on a website. You don't know where the text is stored, who can read it, or whether it's used to train a model. A phone number or a name, once pasted, can't be taken back.

Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019 asks organisations to collect only what they need and keep it secure. The Lakeside Mart privacy policy in our folder says the same. Analysts use customer numbers and leave names out, and they share summaries only.

So at work, ask yourself before every paste. Do I control this tool? If the answer is no, use a made up example or a summary. In this course everything is fictional, so you're safe to practise freely.

## Task 6. Search by meaning (Colab only, needs internet)
Run the sentence-transformers version of the search. This cell downloads a model of about 90 MB the first time. Score it on your test sheet. Your result will differ from the tuned word method.

cells.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
vectors = model.encode([p for n, p in passages], normalize_embeddings=True)

def retrieve3(question):
    qv = model.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    scores = vectors @ qv
    i = int(scores.argmax())
    return passages[i], round(float(scores[i]), 2)

r3 = score(tests, retrieve3)
print((r3.policy == r3.got).sum(), 'of 12 right policy;', r3.answer_found.sum(), 'answers found')

from transformers import pipeline
generate = pipeline('text-generation',
    model='Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct')
RULE = 'Answer only from the passage. Else say so.'
def answer(question):
    (name, passage), s = retrieve2(question)
    text = f'Passage: {passage}\nQuestion: {question}'
    msgs = [{'role': 'system', 'content': RULE},
            {'role': 'user', 'content': text}]
    out = generate(msgs, max_new_tokens=60,
                   do_sample=False)
    return out[0]['generated_text'][-1]['content']
print(answer('How long do points last?'))
